editorial_contributions.text: This paper presents two efficient algorithms for drawing plane graphs nicely. Both draw all edges of a graph as straight line segments without crossing lines. The first draws a plane graph ''convex'' if possible, that is, in a way that every inner face and the complement of the outer face are convex polygons. The second, using the first, procedures a pleasing of a given plane graph that satisfies the following property as far as possible: the complements of 3-connected components, together with inner faces and the complement of the outer face, are convex polygons. The running time and storage space of both algorithms are linear in the number of vertices of the graph.

editorial_contributions.text:
Let \((S,d)\) be a metric space such that \(S\) is a surface and let \(G\) be a connected graph on \(S\) such that each face has diameter 1, is homeomorphic to an open disc and is bounded by a cycle in \(G\). A coloring of \(S\) obtained from \(G\) is called a nice coloring if each color class is the union of faces (and part of their boundaries) such that the distance between any two such faces is greater than 1. It is proved that every nice coloring of \(S\) needs at least 7 colors, provided there exists a natural number \(k\) such that (i), (ii) and (ii) below hold. (i) Every noncontractible simple closed curve has diameter at least 2. (ii) If \(C\) is a simple closed curve of diameter less than 2, then the area of the interior of \(C\) is at most \(k.\) (iii) The diameter of \(S\) is at least \(12k+30.\)


If any one of the three conditions is dropped, then the number of colors needed may decrease.

title.title: Are there any nicely structured preference profiles nearby?

editorial_contributions.text:
[For the entire collection see Zbl 0745.00051.]


The author introduces the notion of proper linearizability by output- feedback, which basically means that feedback linearization can be found, such that the relationship between the new input and the output is linear. A bounded-state-bounded-output (BSBO) nonlinear element affects the linear element, which in turn affects a bounded-input-bounded-state (BIBS) nonlinear element. The nonlinear elements do not affect the linear behavior between the new input and the output. Definitions of BIBS and BSBO are given in Appendix A.


The linearizing compensator is termed normal if the resulting linear system is externally equivalent to a linear system which is tangent to the original nonlinear system at an operating point.


A model is a nicely nonlinear model, if it is tangent to the real nonlinear system at an operating point and properly linearizable by output-feedback.


The author then remarks, that \(a\) if a normal linearizing compensator is applied in an inner loop and then a typical linear compensator designed by classical design methods (based on linearizing the plant at an operating point, etc.) is applied in an outer loop, then the system should perform well over the nonlinear operation of the nicely nonlinear plant model.


Further, that the existence of a smooth linearizing compensator implies the existence of a normal linearizing compensator for a nicely nonlinear plant model. An outline of the proof in Appendix B.


The author then states three main objects involved in the nicely nonlinear modelling problem for a given plant, namely: the data set and set of experiments, a parameterized class of nicely nonlinear models and the model selection criterion. He also notes that these three objects cannot be chosen independently.


The author finally cites two examples. The first one deals with a nonlinear system composed of polynomials preceding apparently linear transfer functions. This system can be feedback linearized in a rather trivial way, assuming one of the polynomials is invertible.


The second example deals briefly with the describing function approach and discusses the well-known assumption of low pass filtering effects of the plant, thus leading to possibly inaccurate results for very low frequencies.


The reviewer finds the paper and the notion of nicely nonlinear modelling and control interesting. Some of the points discussed are rather trivial from an engineering point of view.

editorial_contributions.text: A space is said to be metrizably fibered if it maps continuously and with metrizable fibers onto a metric space. The class \({\mathcal M}\) of metrizably fibered compact spaces is a subclass of the class \({\mathcal {FC}}\) of first-countable compact spaces. It is shown that \({\mathcal M}\) is properly contained in \({\mathcal {FC}}\). Further \({\mathcal M}\) is invariant with respect to open maps but not invariant with respect to continuous maps. It is shown that if a perfectly normal compact space is metrizably fibered then so are all of its continuous images. The notion of a space being weakly metrizably fibered is introduced and it is shown that any Eberlein compact space of weight less than or equal to the continuum is weakly metrizably fibered, while under the negation of the Souslin hypothesis there exist perfectly normal Corson compact spaces of cardinality \(\omega_1\) which are not weakly metrizably fibered.

editorial_contributions.text:
Let \(X\) be a Tychonoff space and \(Y\subseteq X\). The paper studies the locally convex space \(C_p(Y|X)\) consisting of restrictions to \(Y\) of continuous functions on \(X\), endowed with the topology inherited from \(C_p(Y)\).

The main result proves that \(C_p(Y|X)\) is always a large subspace of \(C_p(Y)\). As consequences, the authors show that both spaces have the same strong dual and bidual, that \(C_p(Y|X)\) is always quasibarrelled, and that it is distinguished if and only if \(C_p(Y)\) is distinguished. They also characterize the Montel property by proving that \(C_p(Y|X)\) is Montel precisely when \(Y\) is discrete and \(C\)-embedded in \(X\).

The Stieltjes polynomials \(E_{n+1}^{\lambda}=z^{n+1}+\ldots\) arise from the asymptotic relation 
\[
 1/q_n^{\lambda}(z)=\kappa_{\lambda,n}E_{n+1}^{\lambda}(z)+O(1/z), \quad z\to\infty 
\]
 for the \(n\)-th function of the second kind \(q_n^{\lambda}\), associated to the ultraspherical weight function \(w_\lambda(x)=(1-x^2)^{\lambda-1/2}\), \(\lambda>-1/2\). The authors study the properties of zeros of Stieltjes polynomials in the case when \(\lambda<0\) and show that all of them but two belong to \((-1,1)\), and they strictly interlace with the zeros of the corresponding ultraspherical polynomials. The Gauss--Kronrod quadrature formula is obtained, and the coefficients of such formulae are proved to be positive. An asymptotic representation of the Stieltjes polynomials which converges uniformly on \([-1,1]\) is provided.

The present work provides a parametrized version of the Ky Fan theorem. More precisely the authors consider \(n\)-dimensional sphere bundles \(S^n\to E\stackrel{\pi} \to B\) which arise from vector bundles. They define similar data as in the case of the classical theorem, like triangulations, coloring, etc. Let \(\Diamond^{N}: = \mathrm{conv}\{\pm e_1, \dots, \pm e_N \} \subset \mathbb{R}^N\) be the \(N\)-dimensional cross-polytope whose vertices \(\pm e_i\) are (signed versions of) standard basic vectors \(e_i\) in \(\mathbb{R}^N\) and assume that there is a labeling (coloring) 
\[
\lambda : \mathrm{Vert}(E)\to \{\pm 1,\dots, \pm N\}
\]
which is antipodal with respect to the involution. Then \(\lambda\) yields a simplicial antipodal mapping 
\[
\Lambda : E \to \partial \Diamond^N.
\]
Although the triangulation is not assumed to restrict to a triangulation to each fibre, it is assumed that the projection mapping \(\pi\) is linear on each of the simplices of \(E\). The results are given in terms of the number of simplices called ``\textit{\(i\)-effective}'', which are the simplices \(\sigma\) in \(E\) such that \(\mathrm{Alt}(\sigma)\geq n + i\). Let \(\mathrm{pr}_{n+i-1} : \mathbb{R}^N \to e^{\perp}_{n+i-1}\) be the projection to the orthogonal complement of \(e_{n+i-1}\). Denote by \(Z_i\) the zero set of the composition \(\mathrm{pr}_{n+i-1} \circ \Lambda\). The main results are:

\textbf{Theorem 2}: Let \(\Lambda \to \partial\Diamond ^N\) be a nice coloring of an \(n\)-dimensional sphere bundle \(\pi: E \to B\), where the base \(B\) is a closed compact smooth manifold of dimension \(k\). Then
\begin{itemize}
\item[1.] \(Z_0\) is a pure regular cell complex, a pseudomanifold of dimension \(k\). Its cells are in bijection with the \(i\)-effective simplices.
\item[2.] The induced mapping \[\pi^* : H^*(B) \to H^*(Z_0)\] is a monomorphism.
\item[3.] The pushforward \(\pi_* : H_i(Z_0) \to H_i(B)\) is surjective.
\item[4.] The number of \(n\)-dimensional \(0\)-effective simplices is at least \(k + 1\).
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Theorem 3}: Let \(\Lambda : E \to \partial \Diamond^N\) be a nice coloring of an \(n\)-dimensional sphere bundle \(\pi: E \to B\), where \(\dim(B) = k\). Assume in addition that the height of the first Stiefel-Whitney class of the bundle
\[
E \times_{Z_2} \mathbb{R}^1 \to E/\mathbb{Z}_2
\] 
is at least \(n + i\), i.e., 
\[
0\ne t_{E}^{n+i} \in H^*(E/\mathbb{Z}_2, \mathbb{Z}_2).
\]

Then
\begin{itemize}
\item[1.] \(Z_i\) is a nonempty cycle representing a nontrivial homology class in \(H_{k-i}((E/\mathbb{Z}_2),\mathbb{Z}_2)\).
\item[2.] \(Z_i\) is a pure \((k -i)\)-dimensional regular cell complex, whose cells are in bijection with \(i\)-effective simplices.
\item[3.] The number of \(n + i\)-dimensional \(i\)-effective simplices is at least \(k + 1 - i\).
\end{itemize}

Many explicit examples are provided in the last section. They include spherical bundles associated to the tangent bundles of selected real and complex projective spaces.

editorial_contributions.text:
Let \(R\) be a commutative ring with identity. An ideal \(I\) of \(R\) is called an SFT-ideal if there exist a natural number \(k\) and a finitely generated ideal \(F\subseteq I\) such that \(x^k\in F\) for each \(x\in I\). An SFT-ring is a ring in which every ideal is an SFT-ideal. Let \(R[[X_1,\dots,X_n]]\) be the ring of formal power series in \(n\) variables. An ideal \(\mathcal{I}\) of \(R[[X_1,\dots,X_n]]\) is said nicely-contractible if \((\mathcal{I}\cap R)[[X_1,\dots,X_n]] \subseteq \mathcal{I}\); i.e, a power series with coefficients in \(\mathcal{I}\) belongs to \(\mathcal{I}\). Using the nicely-contractible concept, the author gives equivalent conditions for a ring \(R\) to be an SFT-ring. Let \(R\) be a ring and \(n\in\mathbb{N}^*\). The author shows that the following assertions are equivalent:
\begin{itemize}
\item[1.] All the prime ideals of \(A[[X_1,\dots,X_n]]\) are nicely-contractible.
\item[2.] All the proper radical ideals of \(A[[X_1,\dots,X_n]]\) are nicely-contractible.
\item[3.] The ring \(A\) satisfies the SFT property.
\end{itemize}
The author closes the paper by giving a relation between the \(z\)-ideals of the ring \(R[[X_1,\dots,X_n]]\), of formal power series in finitely many variables and those of \(A\). First, let us recall some concepts. Let \(R\) be a ring and \(n\in\mathbb{N}^*\). If \(S\subseteq R\), we denote by \(M_S\) the intersection of the maximal ideals of \(R\) containing \(S\) and if \(S\subseteq R[[X_1,\dots,X_n]]\), we denote by \(\mathcal{M}_S\) the intersection of the maximal ideals of \(R[[X_1,\dots,X_n]]\) containing \(S\). For a single element \(a\in R\), we use the notation \(M_a\) and for \(f\in R[[X_1,\dots,X_n]]\), we use \(\mathcal{M}_f\). Let \(I\) be a proper ideal of \(R\). We say that \(I\) is an \(z\)-ideal of \(R\) if for each \(a\in I\), we have \(M_a\subseteq I\). Also, we say that \(I\) is an \(sz\)-ideal of \(R\) if for each finite subset \(S\) of \(I\), we have \(M_S\subseteq I\). Let \(R\) be a ring, \(n\in\mathbb{N}^*\) and \(\mathcal{I}\) an ideal of \(R[[X_1,\dots,X_n]]\). The author shows that \(\mathcal{I}\) is an \(z\)-ideal (resp. \(sz\)-ideal) of \(R[[X_1,\dots,X_n]]\) if and only if there exists an \(z\)-ideal (resp. \(sz\)-ideal) \(I\) of \(R\) such that \(\mathcal{I}=I+(X_1,\dots,X_n)R[[X_1,\dots,X_n]]\).

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: A connected graph \(\Gamma\) is called nicely distance-balanced, whenever there exists a positive integer \(\gamma=\gamma(\Gamma)\) such that, for any two adjacent vertices \(u, v\) of \(\Gamma\), there are exactly \(\gamma\) vertices of \(\Gamma\) which are closer to \(u\) than to \(v\), and exactly \(\gamma\) vertices of \(\Gamma\) which are closer to \(v\) than to \(u\). Let \(d\) denote the diameter of \(\Gamma\). It is known that \(d \leq \gamma\), and that nicely distance-balanced graphs with \(\gamma = d\) are precisely complete graphs and cycles of length \(2d\) or \(2d+1\). In this paper we classify regular nicely distance-balanced graphs with \(\gamma=d+1\).

editorial_contributions.text:
Let \((K,v)\) be a Henselian valued field with residue field \(\widehat K\) and value group \(v(K)\). Assume also that \(D\) is a central division \(K\)-algebra of finite dimension \([D:K]\). It is well-known that \(v\) is uniquely, up to equivalence, extendable to a valuation \(v_D\) of \(D\). This also applies to the following results: (i) the value group \(v(D)\) of \((D,v_D)\) is Abelian and contains \(v(K)\) as a subgroup of finite index \(e(D/K)\); (ii) the residue division ring \(\widehat D\) of \((D,v_D)\) is an algebra over \(\widehat K\) of finite dimension \([\widehat D:\widehat K]\); (iii) \([D:K]\) is divisible by \([\widehat D:\widehat K]e(D/K)\).

 The division \(K\)-algebra \(D\) is called defectless, if \([D:K]=[\widehat D:\widehat K]e(D/K)\); we say that \(D\) is nicely semiramified, if it possesses maximal subfields \(L_1\) and \(L_2\), such that \(L_1\) is totally ramified of radical type and \(L_2\) is inertial over \(K\) [see \textit{B. Jacob, A. Wadsworth}, J. Algebra 128, No. 1, 126-179 (1990; Zbl 0692.16011)]. The paper under review shows that if \(D\) is defectless, then it is nicely semiramified if and only if it is split by inertial and by totally ramified field extensions of \(K\).
